title: The Notebooks Became Evidence
subtitle: The Great Terror in the Soviet Union, Moscow and beyond, 1936–1938
intro: In 1937 and 1938 alone, by the usual estimates drawn from the Soviet archives, the state arrested about a million and a half people and shot roughly 680,000 of them. The public face of the Terror was three Moscow show trials — Zinoviev and Kamenev in August 1936, Pyatakov and Radek in January 1937, Bukharin, Rykov and Yagoda in March 1938 — together with the secret trial and execution of Marshal Tukhachevsky and other commanders in June 1937. Its hidden mass was the 'mass operations' launched by NKVD order no. 00447 at the start of August 1937, with quotas for arrest and execution by region, which ran until the Politburo stopped them on 17 November 1938.

This chapter sets diaries from inside that machine beside reports from foreigners who watched it from the courtroom gallery. Its strangest feature is that several of the diaries survive only because the police kept them. Nina Lugovskaya's schoolgirl notebooks, Andrei Arzhilovsky's peasant diary and Yulia Piatnitskaya's diary were confiscated at their arrests and used as evidence; investigators underlined the incriminating lines. They came out of the files after 1987–1991.

The eyes span the whole range of belief. Georgi Dimitrov wrote down Stalin's words at the Kremlin table without comment. Maria Svanidze, part of Stalin's family circle, called the fallen 'chameleons' months before she fell herself. Nina Kosterina promised not to pity a traitor father, then saw her father taken. Alexander Afinogenov, denounced but never arrested, used his diary to remake himself, while Stepan Podlubny tried for years to write away a kulak origin. Lyubov Shaporina in Leningrad wrote privately what few dared to think.

Three foreigners frame the trials. Lion Feuchtwanger, the exiled German novelist, and Joseph Davies, the American ambassador, both found the confessions plausible; Fitzroy Maclean of the British embassy, writing a decade later, did not. Their accounts are dated letters, a travel report and a memoir rather than diaries, and are tagged that way. Davies's and Feuchtwanger's sympathy for the prosecution is flagged where it appears, not argued with.

Because these are modern publications, nothing is quoted: every entry is a paraphrase. Where an exact entry date could not be checked, the date of the event is given and the entry is marked approximate. Three 'entries' are not entries at all but the day a diary was seized; they are labelled so, because in this chapter the end of a diary is part of its story.
calendar_note: Soviet Russia adopted the Gregorian calendar in February 1918, so all dates here are as the diarists wrote them; no conversion is needed.

eyes.name: Nina Sergeevna Lugovskaya
eyes.role: Moscow schoolgirl, 18 in January 1937; daughter of a man repeatedly arrested and exiled (most recently in 1935)
eyes.side: Soviet citizens; a family already marked by the police
eyes.vantage_label: direct victim — her diary became the evidence
eyes.authenticity: Kept 1932–1937. Confiscated in the NKVD search of 4 January 1937 and kept in the family's case file, where investigators had underlined the passages they meant to use. Found in the archive after 1991 by Irina Osipova of Memorial and published in Moscow (2003); English editions 2003 (Glas) and 2007 ('I Want to Live', tr. Andrew Bromfield), which prints the NKVD's underlined passages in bold. Published under her own name.
eyes.bio: A sharp, unhappy, clever teenager who disliked the Komsomol slogans of her teachers and loved her persecuted father. Her diary is the purest case of a private notebook turned into a prosecution file: the police read it and marked it before any outsider did. She, her mother and two sisters were sentenced to five years in Kolyma; she was freed in 1942, stayed in exile in the far north-east, was rehabilitated in 1963 and became a painter.

sources.title: Nina Lugovskaya — biography, arrest, publication history
I Want to Live (Black Swan edition, publisher page)
Russian Life — final diary entries before arrest (Lugovskaya, Arzhilovsky, Svanidze, Piatnitskaya and others)

eyes.name: Nina Alekseevna Kosterina
eyes.role: Moscow schoolgirl and Komsomol member, 16 in 1937
eyes.side: Soviet citizens; a loyal young communist
eyes.vantage_label: eyewitness — loyal schoolgirl whose father was taken
eyes.authenticity: Kept from 1936 until her death in 1941. Kept by the family; published in a Soviet magazine in 1962 during the Khrushchev thaw, as a book in 1964, and in English in 1968 ('The Diary of Nina Kosterina', tr. Mirra Ginsburg). As a thaw-era publication it may have been edited; no manuscript comparison was checked here.
eyes.bio: The mirror of Lugovskaya: the same age, the same city, but a believer. She wrote that she would not pity a traitor even if it were her own father — and then her father, the writer and old revolutionary Alexei Kosterin, was arrested on 6 May 1938 and sent to Kolyma. She volunteered for a partisan unit in 1941 and was killed behind German lines that December.

sources.title: Nina Kosterina — biography and publication history
Alexei Kosterin — arrest of 6 May 1938
Radio Svoboda — 1937 diaries (Kosterina, Svanidze, Arzhilovsky)

eyes.name: Andrei Stepanovich Arzhilovsky
eyes.role: Peasant in the Chervishevo district near Tyumen, western Siberia; a former prisoner released in 1936
eyes.vantage_label: direct victim — far from Moscow, caught by the mass operations
eyes.authenticity: Diary of 1936–37, confiscated at his arrest on 29 August 1937 and kept in his case file. Published in the journal 'Ural' (no. 3, 1992) and in English in 'Intimacy and Terror: Soviet Diaries of the 1930s' (Garros, Korenevskaya, Lahusen, 1995).
eyes.bio: An ageing, sardonic peasant writing about weather, crops, hunger and his sons, with flashes of open contempt for the collective farm order. The diary was seized when he was arrested and he was shot on 5 September 1937 as a member of a 'kulak sabotage group' — one of the hundreds of thousands caught in the mass operations under order no. 00447. He shows that the Terror was not only a Moscow story.

sources.title: Russian Life — Arzhilovsky's 27 June 1937 entry, arrest and execution dates
Tyumen State University Herald — 'Truthful dreams of Andrey Arzhilovskiy' (2022)
Intimacy and Terror (The New Press)

eyes.name: Yulia Iosifovna Sokolova-Piatnitskaya
eyes.role: Engineer; wife of the Old Bolshevik and former Comintern leader Osip Piatnitsky
eyes.side: Soviet elite; family of an arrested Bolshevik
eyes.vantage_label: wife of an arrested leader — inside the elite as it fell
eyes.authenticity: Diary kept 1937–38 after her husband's arrest; it was used against her when she herself was arrested on 27 October 1938. Published abroad as 'Dnevnik zheny bol'shevika' (Benson, Vermont: Chalidze Publications, 1987). Exact first-entry date not checked; entries below dated from the event are marked approx.
eyes.bio: A believing communist who, after her husband's arrest, tries to understand how a man she knew could be an enemy — and records the slow loss of work, friends and her son. Her son Igor was arrested in February 1938. She was sentenced to five years in the camps and died there in 1940. Her husband, a founder of the Comintern's organising apparatus, was shot.

sources.title: Russian Life — Piatnitskaya's 28 May 1938 entry and arrest
Russian Life — Osip Piatnitsky caption (arrest 7 July 1937; son's arrest)

eyes.name: Maria Anisimovna Svanidze
eyes.role: Singer; wife of Alexander Svanidze, brother of Stalin's first wife — a member of Stalin's family circle
eyes.vantage_label: at Stalin's table — the court seen from within
eyes.authenticity: Diary 1933–1937, published in Russia in 1993 ('Iosif beskonechno dobr…', in 'Dokumenty russkoi istorii'). The last entry is dated 7 August 1937. She and her husband were arrested at the end of 1937; she was shot in 1942.
eyes.bio: She dined with Stalin and adored him, and her diary records the arrests of people she knew as the unmasking of 'chameleons'. Within months she and her husband were themselves arrested. Her angle is the court's own: belief, gossip and loyalty, right up to the edge.

sources.title: Radio Svoboda — 7 August 1937 entry and her arrest
Russian Life — Svanidze entry and fate

eyes.name: Alexander Nikolaevich Afinogenov
eyes.where: Moscow and the writers' settlement of Peredelkino
eyes.vantage_label: public figure denounced, waiting to be arrested
eyes.authenticity: His diary for December 1934 to late 1937 survived as working notes for a planned novel ('Three Years'); entries continue into 1938. Excerpts published in Russia and discussed by Jochen Hellbeck ('Revolution on My Mind', 2006). Afinogenov reworked the diary for literary use, so it is partly self-fashioning.
eyes.bio: A star dramatist close to the purged literary bosses Averbakh and Kirshon, he was denounced in spring 1937 and expelled from the party, but never arrested. For months he lived in limbo at Peredelkino, using the diary to purge and remake himself; he was reinstated in early 1938. He was killed in a German air raid on Moscow on 29 October 1941.

sources.title: The Nation — 'Journals of the Purge Years' (Hellbeck's diarists)
Novaya Gazeta — Benedikt Sarnov, 'Strakh' (Afinogenov's diary quoted)

eyes.name: Stepan Filippovich Podlubny
eyes.role: Son of a dekulakised Ukrainian peasant, trying to remake himself as a model Soviet worker and student in Moscow
eyes.side: Soviet citizens; a 'class alien' passing as a proletarian
eyes.vantage_label: same city — hiding a stigmatised past
eyes.authenticity: Diary 1931–1939, studied by Jochen Hellbeck (published in German as 'Tagebuch aus Moskau 1931–1939', 1996, and in 'Revolution on My Mind'). Podlubny himself, in the 1990s, read it as a record of victimisation. Entries below are month-level and approx.
eyes.bio: He kept the diary 'for his overall development', to turn himself into a new Soviet man and bury his kulak origins; the secret police recruited him as an informer in 1932. His origins came out in early 1936 and he lost his Komsomol membership and his place at medical school; in December 1937 his mother was arrested. He is the diarist who most clearly tried to think like the regime about himself.

sources.title: The Nation — 'Journals of the Purge Years'

eyes.name: Lyubov Vasilievna Shaporina
eyes.role: Founder of the Leningrad puppet theatre, translator; wife of the composer Yuri Shaporin
eyes.side: Old intelligentsia; privately hostile to the regime
eyes.vantage_label: Leningrad — the same terror in the second city
eyes.authenticity: Long diary (1898–1967); 1930s excerpts in 'Intimacy and Terror' (1995) and a full Russian edition later. The excerpts show some later interpolation (the chronology of the November 1937 section is confused). Dates below follow the 'Intimacy and Terror' excerpt as summarised by SIUE's music-history site.
eyes.bio: The most openly anti-Soviet voice here, and one of the most precise: she lists arrested friends, counts what the city stops saying aloud, and listens at night. She kept writing through the siege of Leningrad, when she worked as a hospital nurse.

sources.title: SIUE (Aho) — Lyubov Shaporina's diary, dated excerpts 1936–1938
SIUE — notes on Shaporina's diary

eyes.name: Georgi Dimitrov
eyes.role: Bulgarian communist; General Secretary of the Communist International (Comintern) in Moscow
eyes.authenticity: Working diary 1933–1949, written in German, Russian and Bulgarian. English edition: 'The Diary of Georgi Dimitrov, 1933–1949', ed. Ivo Banac (Yale University Press, Annals of Communism, 2003). Terse, with direct notes of Stalin's words.
eyes.bio: Hero of the 1933 Leipzig Reichstag-fire trial, then head of the Comintern as it was purged around him. His diary is the nearest thing to a record of what Stalin said privately while the Terror ran: brief notes, almost no comment. Many of the foreign communists he worked with were arrested; he survived and led Bulgaria after the war.

sources.title: Yale University Press — The Diary of Georgi Dimitrov, 1933–1949
Robert Fulford review (2003)
Oberender, Zeitgeschichte-online (2008) — Dimitrov diary and the 7 Nov 1937 toast

eyes.name: Joseph Edward Davies
eyes.role: United States Ambassador to the Soviet Union, 1936–1938
eyes.where: US Embassy (Spaso House) and the trial courtroom, Moscow
eyes.authenticity: Dated dispatches, letters and journal notes published in 'Mission to Moscow' (Simon & Schuster, 1941), selected and arranged by Davies for a wartime audience; some official cables are also in FRUS. Flag: Davies's view of the trials was favourable to the prosecution — he came to accept the confessions as largely genuine, a judgement most historians now reject. The book was later made into a 1943 Hollywood film.
eyes.bio: A wealthy Washington lawyer and Roosevelt loyalist with no Russian, sent to Moscow in late 1936. He attended the Pyatakov–Radek trial in January 1937 and the Bukharin trial in March 1938 and reported on both. His cables are cautious; his published book is warmer to the Soviet case. He matters as the outsider who believed.

sources.title: Davies, 'Behind the Moscow Trials', dispatch of 17 Feb 1937 (Seventeen Moments in Soviet History)
FRUS, The Soviet Union 1933–1939, doc. 453 — Davies telegram, 2 March 1938

eyes.name: Lion Feuchtwanger
eyes.role: German-Jewish novelist in exile in France; guest of the Soviet Writers' Union
eyes.vantage_label: foreign writer, invited guest at the trial
eyes.authenticity: 'Moskau 1937' is a travel report written within weeks of his return and published by Querido in Amsterdam in 1937 (Russian edition the same year). Not a diary. Flag: a sympathetic account written partly as a reply to André Gide's critical 'Return from the USSR'; it accepts the trials as plausible.
eyes.bio: Germany's best-selling exiled novelist saw Stalin's USSR as the one great power standing against Hitler. He spent about ten weeks in Moscow, had a two-hour interview with Stalin, and sat in the Pyatakov trial. His book is valuable precisely for what an intelligent anti-fascist chose to believe.

sources.title: der Freitag — 'Moskau 1937: Im Kreml hat Lion Feuchtwanger einen Termin bei Stalin'
Moscou, 1937 — Portuguese translation, preface (Marxists Internet Archive)

eyes.name: Fitzroy Maclean
eyes.role: Junior British diplomat at the Moscow embassy, 1937–1939
eyes.where: British Embassy and the trial courtroom, Moscow
eyes.authenticity: 'Eastern Approaches' (London, 1949; US edition 'Escape to Adventure', 1950), written a decade later, devotes some forty pages to the March 1938 trial. Flag: a later memoir with novelist's shaping, not a contemporary diary; no exact daily dates are used here.
eyes.bio: A 27-year-old Scot who later became famous as Churchill's envoy to Tito. He attended every day of the Trial of the Twenty-One and wrote one of the most vivid outside accounts of Bukharin, Yagoda and the others in the dock. Sceptical where Davies was credulous.

sources.title: Eastern Approaches (book article)
Fitzroy Maclean — biography

entries.headline: His kulak origins found out
entries.digest: The past he had hidden for years caught up with him: his file revealed that he was the son of a dekulakised peasant. He was expelled from the Komsomol and lost the stipend that kept him at medical school. After writing it down he stopped keeping the diary for the rest of 1936.
entries.source_note: The Nation, 'Journals of the Purge Years' (Hellbeck): exposure in early 1936; silence for the rest of 1936. Exact entry date not seen.

entries.headline: A dream about Stalin, written down
entries.digest: He recorded a dream in which a drunken Stalin attacked a bearded man, and the dreamer was afraid the same would be done to him. He wrote it down as a curiosity. Eight months later the police would have the notebook in which it appears.
entries.source_note: Radio Svoboda article quoting the diary, entry of 18.12.1936; 'Ural' 1992.

entries.headline: An exiled novelist arrives as an honoured guest
entries.digest: He arrived in Moscow at the invitation of the Writers' Union for a stay of about ten weeks. He came as a sympathiser, looking for the great counterweight to Nazi Germany, but he also arrived with questions about the personality cult and the trial of the previous August.
entries.source_note: der Freitag (Herden): stay December 1936 – February 1937; exact arrival day not given.

entries.headline: New Year with friends — the last entry
entries.digest: She described seeing in the New Year with friends: wine, warmth, and an unusual sense of belonging. It is one of the last things she wrote. The next night the police came to search the flat.
entries.source_note: Russian Life, 'Final diary entries before arrest' (entry of 3 Jan 1937, from 'Khochu zhit'', Moscow 2003).

entries.headline: The diary is seized and read by the police
entries.digest: Not an entry: this is the night the diary stopped. In an NKVD search of the family flat the notebooks were confiscated. Investigators went through them and underlined her complaints about school indoctrination, her loyalty to her father, her dark moods and her wish that someone would kill Stalin. The marked pages became the case against her; she was arrested on 16 March.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, 'Nina Lugovskaya' (search of 4 Jan 1937; underlined passages); Russian Life (arrest 16 March 1937). Event, not a diary entry.

entries.headline: Two hours with Stalin
entries.digest: He was received by Stalin in the Kremlin for about two hours. He raised the cult of personality and the trials; he came away judging Stalin a frank, sober man who disliked the adulation around him, an impression he put into his book.
entries.source_note: der Freitag gives the morning of 7 January 1937; other accounts give 8 January. Content from 'Moskau 1937' as summarised there.

entries.headline: In the gallery at the Pyatakov trial
entries.digest: Stalin had offered him a seat, and he watched the trial of Pyatakov, Radek and fifteen others. He found the atmosphere relaxed, more like a discussion than a tribunal, and the defendants calm. He asked himself whether it was theatre and concluded he could not know; he thought it plausible that old oppositionists had worked with the Soviet Union's enemies.
entries.source_note: der Freitag summary of 'Moskau 1937'; trial opened 23 January 1937.

entries.headline: The new ambassador attends the Radek–Pyatakov trial
entries.digest: Only weeks into his post, Davies sat through the trial with an interpreter. He noticed that most of the seventeen accused were secondary figures and that the confessions were detailed and calm. He set out his conclusions in a long dispatch three weeks later.
entries.source_note: Davies, 'Behind the Moscow Trials', dispatch of 17 Feb 1937, 'Mission to Moscow' pp. 32–53 (Seventeen Moments site).

entries.headline: The trial read as a staged confession
entries.digest: On the day the Pyatakov verdicts were published, she wrote about the trial as a public confession put on for the country. To her the performance said more about the regime that staged it than about the accused.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, entry of 30 Jan 1937, as summarised on SIUE (Aho) Shaporina page.

entries.headline: 'Behind the Moscow Trials' — a dispatch to Washington
entries.digest: In a confidential report to the Secretary of State he traced the case from Kirov's murder in 1934 through the Zinoviev–Kamenev trial of August 1936. He described the defendants as lifelong conspirators, explained the harsh Soviet code on crimes against the state, and leaned towards accepting that a real plot had existed. (Flag: his view of the trials was far more favourable to the prosecution than that of most diplomats.)
entries.source_note: Seventeen Moments in Soviet History, 'Behind the Moscow Trials' (dated 17 Feb 1937; page header gives 1 Feb).

entries.headline: Denounced as an 'enemy of the people'
entries.digest: With his patrons Averbakh and Kirshon under arrest, the playwright found himself attacked in print and at meetings, and was expelled from the party. His diary turns inward: he treats the disgrace as a test and a chance to rebuild himself, while waiting every night for a knock that never came.
entries.source_note: The Nation (Hellbeck): denounced spring 1937; expelled but not arrested. Exact dates of entries not seen.

entries.headline: Warm rain at last, and too little to eat
entries.digest: After a long cold spell the weather turned warm and wet, and he hoped for mushrooms. He had been working hard in the fields, scolding his impractical sons without effect, and worrying about the younger, timid children who were bullied by others. The family was living half-starved. Two months later he was arrested.
entries.source_note: Russian Life, entry of 27 June 1937 (from 'Ural', 1992, no. 3).

entries.headline: Her husband is taken
entries.digest: Osip Piatnitsky, a Bolshevik since before the revolution and for years a leader of the Comintern, was arrested. Her diary from these months is an attempt to reconcile the man she lived with and the enemy the newspapers now described; she does not yet doubt the party, only her own judgement.
entries.source_note: Russian Life caption (arrest 7 July 1937). The exact date of her first entry on it was not checked in the 1987 edition.

entries.headline: 'Chameleons' — the court's view of the arrests
entries.digest: In what turned out to be her last entry, she wrote that the people being unmasked were chameleons who could never accept the Soviet order and who would betray and hate it. She was shaken by how many familiar faces had fallen in about a year, but explained it the way Stalin's circle did. Within months she and her husband were arrested too.
entries.source_note: Radio Svoboda (entry of 7 Aug 1937, her last); Russian Life (arrest December 1937).

entries.headline: A friend's father arrested — and her own resolve
entries.digest: When the father of a girl she knew was arrested as a Trotskyist, she wrote that if her own father turned out to be a traitor she would not pity him. Even as she wrote it she admitted to doubt. The mass operations under order no. 00447 had begun only weeks before.
entries.source_note: Radio Svoboda, entry of 22.08.1937.

entries.headline: Living inside 'The Last Day of Pompeii'
entries.digest: She compared the summer to Bryullov's painting of the eruption that buried Pompeii: the columns falling one by one around her and no way out. It is a painter's image for a time when arrests came to her own circle.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 27 Aug 1937 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: Arrested; the diary goes to the investigators
entries.digest: Not an entry: the day the diary ended. He was arrested and the notebook was confiscated and added to his file. On 5 September 1937 he was shot as a member of a 'kulak sabotage group'. The diary survived only because the police kept it.
entries.source_note: Russian Life (arrest and confiscation 29 Aug; shot 5 Sept 1937). Event, not a diary entry.

entries.headline: Writing his own interrogation
entries.digest: Alone at the writers' settlement, he began a dialogue in the diary written as the record of an interrogation, imagining the questions and answers he expected to face. It is a rehearsal of arrest by a man who knew how plays are built.
entries.source_note: Novaya Gazeta (Sarnov) on the 'protocol of interrogation' begun in early September 1937.

entries.headline: How calmly people speak of shootings
entries.digest: She was struck by how evenly people around her now talked about executions, as if discussing the weather. She made a list of acquaintances who had been arrested or shot.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 10 Oct 1937 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: Gunfire in the night by the fortress
entries.digest: She heard shooting through the night from the direction of the Peter and Paul Fortress and wondered whether it was executions. She could not know, and she wrote down the not-knowing.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 22 Oct 1937 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: A friend arrested, her daughters taken into state care
entries.digest: She recorded the arrest of a woman she knew and the removal of the woman's young daughters to a state children's reception centre. The editors note the chronology of this section is confused, suggesting later additions.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, dated 2 Nov 1937; editors flag possible interpolation (pp. 355–6), per SIUE.

entries.headline: Stalin's toast on the anniversary of the revolution
entries.digest: At the holiday dinner after the parade, Stalin gave a long toast promising to destroy every enemy of the state completely, even an old Bolshevik, together with his family. Dimitrov noted the words and the approval of those present, and pledged to carry the same fight into the Comintern. He added no comment of his own.
entries.source_note: Banac ed., Diary of Georgi Dimitrov, entry 7.XI.1937, as cited by Oberender (2008) and Fulford (2003).

entries.headline: Stalin names names in the Comintern
entries.digest: In a meeting Stalin went through foreign communists to be arrested, remarking that the veteran Elena Stasova would probably be taken too. He also told Dimitrov that conspirators had planned an attack on the Politburo in the Kremlin, a story Dimitrov seems to have found plausible. (Stasova was in fact spared.)
entries.source_note: Fulford review (11 Nov 1937 conversation); Oberender footnote.

entries.headline: Shostakovich's Fifth: an audience in tears
entries.digest: At the Leningrad Philharmonic premiere of Shostakovich's Fifth Symphony she watched the audience react with intense emotion, a long ovation that seemed to her to carry everything people could not say aloud.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 21 Nov 1937 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: Everyone waits for the night
entries.digest: She wrote that people now lived in a permanent state of fear, going to bed each night uncertain whether the doorbell would ring before morning.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 22 Nov 1937 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: One name on the ballot
entries.digest: At the first elections to the Supreme Soviet under the new constitution she found a ballot with a single candidate and thought the whole procedure absurd.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 12 Dec 1937 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: 'A great day' — the expelled playwright votes
entries.digest: Still outside the party, he described election day as festive and solemn, comparing the act of voting to a religious rite whose importance nobody yet grasped. Set beside Shaporina's entry, it shows how differently two writers could see the same ballot.
entries.source_note: Novaya Gazeta (Sarnov) quotes this entry with the date 12 December 1938; the first Supreme Soviet election was on 12 Dec 1937, so the year is taken as 1937.

entries.headline: His mother is arrested
entries.digest: His mother was arrested and later sentenced to eight years. For a young man who had spent years trying to bury his origins, it was the final proof that he could not write himself out of them.
entries.source_note: The Nation (Hellbeck): mother arrested December 1937, sentenced to eight years. Exact entry not seen.

entries.headline: An early-morning arrest, and the children left behind
entries.digest: She recorded the arrest of another friend before dawn and what it did to the children of the household.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 6 Feb 1938 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: 'I have my party card'
entries.digest: After months in limbo he was reinstated and handed back his party card. The diary records relief and gratitude, and a sense that his ordeal had been a necessary cleansing.
entries.source_note: Novaya Gazeta (Sarnov) quotes the entry for 7 February; the year follows from his reinstatement in early 1938 (The Nation).

entries.headline: Her son is taken
entries.digest: Her elder son Igor, a tenth-grader, was arrested. She had already lost her husband and her work; now she spent her days in queues trying to find out where he was held.
entries.source_note: Russian Life caption (Igor arrested 15 Feb 1938). Diary wording not checked.

entries.headline: First day of the Bukharin trial: a sensation in the dock
entries.digest: His cable that evening summarised the indictment against twenty-one defendants — sabotage, spying, plots against Stalin and the deaths of Gorky and others. The sensation of the day was Krestinsky withdrawing his confession and pleading not guilty. Davies called the indictment one-sided and said his judgement would depend on the testimony still to come.
entries.source_note: FRUS, Soviet Union 1933–1939, doc. 453 (telegram of 2 March 1938, 8 p.m.).

entries.headline: Every day of the Trial of the Twenty-One
entries.digest: He attended every session of the trial of Bukharin, Rykov, Yagoda and the others and later gave it some forty pages. He watched the defendants confess to crimes that did not fit together and found the spectacle impossible to believe as a judicial proceeding; he recalled the sense that Stalin himself might be watching unseen.
entries.source_note: 'Eastern Approaches' (1949), written a decade later; attendance per summaries of the book. No single-day dating.

entries.headline: The last great trial, and Russia's fate
entries.digest: As the Moscow trial drew to its close she thought about Russia's history through Dostoevsky — the possessed, the confessions — and what the trial said about the country.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 11 Mar 1938 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: A writer's flat searched
entries.digest: She recorded the search of the writer Elena Tager's flat and her arrest — the start of what became a case against a group of Leningrad writers.
entries.source_note: Intimacy and Terror excerpt, 21 Mar 1938 (SIUE summary).

entries.headline: Her father is arrested
entries.digest: On 6 May 1938 her father, the writer and veteran revolutionary Alexei Kosterin, was arrested and later sentenced to five years in Kolyma. The loyalty she had promised the year before was tested on her own family; the diary continues, and so does her Komsomol life.
entries.source_note: Arrest date from Wikipedia, 'Alexei Kosterin'. The diary's entry on it was not seen; month-level.

entries.headline: Out of work, watched, and grieving
entries.digest: She wrote in despair about being unable to find work and about how the authorities treated her. She described property being confiscated from neighbours, said she no longer trusted the NKVD people she dealt with, and was hurt that her son had taken his father's pen. The day before she had learned that Igor was sentenced to five years in a children's labour colony.
entries.source_note: Russian Life (entry of 28 May 1938; news of Igor's sentence 27 May 1938).

entries.headline: Her own diary becomes the charge
entries.digest: Not an entry: the day the diary ended. She was arrested and charged with anti-Soviet agitation on the basis of what she had written. She was sentenced to five years and died in a camp in 1940. Three weeks later, on 17 November, the regime ordered an end to the mass operations.
entries.source_note: Russian Life (arrest 27 Oct 1938, diary used as evidence; died 1940). Event, not a diary entry.

convergences.label: Pyatakov–Radek trial, 23–30 January 1937
convergences.note: Two invited foreigners in the gallery see composed men making believable confessions; in Leningrad Shaporina, reading the same reports, sees a staged confession. Proximity made the outsiders more credulous, not less.

convergences.label: Order 00447: mass operations begin, August 1937
convergences.note: Within three weeks the Kremlin insider calls the victims chameleons, a Moscow schoolgirl vows not to pity a traitor father, a Leningrad woman feels Pompeii's columns falling — and a Siberian peasant is arrested with his diary in the house.

convergences.label: Twentieth anniversary of the revolution, November 1937
convergences.note: At the Kremlin dinner Stalin promises to destroy enemies and their families; two weeks later in Leningrad Shaporina writes that everyone goes to bed waiting for the doorbell. The same policy, from the top table and from the stairwell.

convergences.label: First Supreme Soviet elections, 12 December 1937
convergences.note: Shaporina finds one name on the ballot and calls it absurd; Afinogenov, expelled and frightened, calls it a great day and a kind of sacrament. Same ballot, opposite readings.

convergences.label: Trial of the Twenty-One (Bukharin), 2–13 March 1938
convergences.note: Two Western diplomats sit in the same hall: Davies cables cautiously but would later accept the case, Maclean finds it unbelievable. Shaporina, far away, reaches for Dostoevsky.

convergences.label: Families of the arrested, spring 1938
convergences.note: In the same month Kosterina's father is taken and Piatnitskaya learns her son's sentence: the believing daughter and the believing wife facing the same wall.

ties.note: Both sat in the Hall of Columns for the Bukharin trial in March 1938 as Western diplomats, and drew opposite conclusions.
Both attended the Pyatakov–Radek trial in January 1937 as foreign observers and both judged the confessions plausible.
Her husband Osip Piatnitsky had been a leading figure of the Comintern apparatus that Dimitrov headed; the Comintern purges that Dimitrov discussed with Stalin swallowed him.
Two Moscow schoolgirls of almost the same age with fathers in trouble: one hostile and whose diary was used against her, one loyal and whose diary was published by the Soviet state in 1962.
Not in life: their diaries were published side by side in 'Intimacy and Terror' (1995), the anthology that first brought these voices to English readers.

threads_out.note: The men in the dock in 1936–38 — Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin, Rykov — and Osip Piatnitsky were Bolsheviks of 1917. The Terror destroyed most of the surviving leadership of the revolution described in the 1917 chapter.

Shaporina kept writing through the siege of Leningrad, the city of Lena Mukhina's siege diary. Afinogenov was killed by a German bomb in Moscow on 29 October 1941, and Kosterina died with a partisan unit behind German lines that December. The army that met the invasion had lost much of its command in 1937–38.

Dimitrov's Comintern organised the International Brigades for the Spanish Republic from autumn 1936. The charge of 'Trotskyism' used in the Moscow trials was turned in 1937 against the POUM and other anti-Stalinist left groups in Republican Spain.

Most of these diaries reached readers only as the Soviet system opened and collapsed. Piatnitskaya's came out abroad in 1987, Arzhilovsky's in 1992, Svanidze's in 1993, and Lugovskaya's was found in her family's NKVD file after 1991.
